title: DST Checker by Coordinates: Offset at a Point
description: Check daylight saving and the UTC offset for exact coordinates with the DST Checker by Coordinates — the point's own rules, not the city's. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, two points in the same state can keep different clocks — Indiana's counties historically split between time zones and rules, and a point-level check is how you know which side you are on.
quick_answer: The DST Checker by Coordinates resolves the timezone for an exact pair of coordinates and reports whether daylight saving applies there, with the offsets in force. Enter the point — a field, a border town, a ship's position — and read its clock rules rather than the nearest big city's.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
The timezone, UTC offsets and DST status for an exact coordinate pair — the point's clock rules from the tz database.
Do I need an account?
No. Coordinates in, clock rules out.
Can I use the result for professional work?
For scheduling, logging and fieldwork planning, yes — it reads the same tz database professionals build on. Payroll and legal deadlines deserve your system's own confirmation too.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — the coordinates you type are the query; your device's location is not involved.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Zone boundaries move with politics; the database's vintage decides the answer. A recently changed border can differ between sources by design.
A point in the ocean?
The tz database assigns ocean zones too (often the nearest land's zone or Etc/GMT bands). The checker reports what the data holds for the point.
Historical dates?
Zone rules have histories — the database knows many of them. A 1990 timestamp at the same point can carry a different offset, and the check respects the date.
Half-hour zones?
Several exist (India, parts of Australia, Newfoundland at -3:30 standard) — the checker reports offsets to the minute, as the database states them.
My city and my point disagree.
Possible near boundaries — trust the point for the point. That disagreement is this page's entire reason to exist.
Does it handle the exact changeover moment?

Transitions are instants in the database (a specific UTC second). A timestamp inside the repeated or skipped hour is genuinely ambiguous — the checker's date-level answer flags the day as a changeover day.
Ships and aircraft?
Their clocks follow conventions and flags, not geography. The checker gives the point's zone answer — the reference the convention is measured against.
